abstract: Pre-registered three-month RCT (AEARCTR-0015823) with 133 practicing patent lawyers at eleven U.S. IP law firms, randomized to a custom Google AI drafting assistant (InFlow) or no access; study period May 2025 through February 2026. Blinded expert patent attorneys scored all work. AI access raised the quality of benchmark patent drafts by 0.34 SD at 10 days (p = 0.03) and 0.38 SD at 90 days (p = 0.01), with larger gains for juniors. On a later unaided redlining task, treated lawyers outperformed controls by 0.32 SD (p = 0.04), but the gain was concentrated among senior lawyers (0.45 SD, p = 0.02); juniors showed no average gain and their scores bifurcated. As a secondary finding, treated participants self-reported finishing the 10-day drafting task about 10 minutes faster against a 112-minute baseline (p = 0.05), roughly 9% less time; the 90-day task showed a similar but insignificant 10-minute saving on a 125-minute base (p = 0.27). Time savings were concentrated among juniors; seniors did not work faster with AI.
keyFindings: +0.34 SD drafting quality at 10 days (p = 0.03) and +0.38 SD at 90 days (p = 0.01) for lawyers with AI access
~9% less time on the 10-day drafting task: 10 minutes saved on a 112-minute baseline (p = 0.05), self-reported
10 minutes saved on a 125-minute base at 90 days, not significant (p = 0.27)
Juniors saved 18 minutes at 10 days (p = 0.05); seniors 5 minutes, indistinguishable from zero (p = 0.35)
+0.32 SD on an unaided redlining task after three months (p = 0.04), concentrated among seniors (+0.45 SD, p = 0.02); juniors no average gain
methodology: Pre-registered RCT, 133 practicing patent lawyers, 11 U.S. IP firms, May 2025–Feb 2026. Treatment: access to Google's pre-release InFlow drafting assistant. Outcomes: blinded expert scoring of benchmark drafting tasks at 10 and 90 days and an unaided redlining task at 90 days; self-reported time per task.
qualifiers: NBER working paper (repo convention: Tier 1). Google funded the direct costs and four co-authors are Google employees or contractors. Time results use self-reported minutes and the authors treat them as context rather than hypothesis tests; the 90-day time effect is not significant. Single occupation, 133 subjects; quality is measured in SD units, not percent.
